RESULT (main analysis executed). Executed script: /workspace/analysis.py; outputs in /workspace/out/.

== HYPOTHESIS (natural-language, data-grounded) ==
The gardening pathway shows different prevalence styles across habitat types in the context of the degree of human modification of the habitat — i.e., the contrast between human-modified / water-adjacent habitats (Urban, Wetlands, Coastal, Riparian) and natural / semi-natural habitats (broad-leaved & coniferous forests, meadows, scrublands, rock outcrops).

- In the HUMAN-MODIFIED + water-adjacent habitats, gardening takes a HIGH-OCCURRENCE / LOW-ABUNDANCE ("widespread but shallow") style: its species are present in many plots (occurrence 0.36–0.50 of plots: Wetlands 0.500, Urban 0.477, Coastal 0.448, Riparian 0.361) but at low per-plot counts (mean ~1.4–1.8 species/occupied plot, max 3–4) and only MODERATE dominance (share of all introduced species 0.30–0.56: Wetlands 0.558, Coastal 0.535, Riparian 0.365, Urban 0.298).
- In the NATURAL habitats, gardening takes a LOW-OCCURRENCE / HIGH-DOMINANCE ("rare but dominant") style: it is found in very few plots (occurrence <0.08: Coniferous 0.065, Meadows 0.077, Broad-leaved 0.044, Scrublands 0.019, Rock outcrops 0.000), yet where it does occur it is often the sole pathway — dominance up to 1.000 (Broad-leaved forests) and 0.875 (Coniferous forests) — simply because total introductions in these habitats are tiny.

So the "context" is: as habitat human-modification / water adjacency increases, gardening's prevalence style flips from rare-but-dominant (natural) to broadly-occurring-but-shallow (modified). This is the OPPOSITE of the unintentional pathway, which is the high-occurrence AND high-abundance style, dominant in Croplands (unintentional share 0.769, 83 species, 0.511 occurrence) and Urban (104 species, 0.689 share). AgriForest is a sparse third comparator (23 total, concentrated in Riparian) and does not form a distinct style.

Cross-check (species-level, invasion_success_pathways.csv): gardening species are fewer and narrower (42 species, mean habitat.range 1.95, mean 3.88 invaded plots, niche breadth 0.455) vs unintentional (30 species, habitat.range 2.77, 9.60 plots, breadth 0.749) — consistent with gardening being a concentrated, habitat-specific pathway.

== STATISTICAL EVIDENCE (from analysis.py) ==
- Kruskal–Wallis on per-plot n.gard across the 10 habitats: H=140.72, p=7.3e-26 (gardening prevalence differs strongly by habitat).
- Chi-square on gardening presence across the 10 habitats: chi2=139.45, p=1.3e-25.
- Fisher exact, gardening presence anthropogenic vs natural: OR=6.15, p=2.3e-17 (gardening ~6x more likely present in modified habitats: 0.366 vs 0.086 of plots).
- Chi-square on pathway composition (gard vs unint) by group: chi2=4.85, dof=1, p=0.028.

== SECONDARY (land-cover) CORROBORATION — HONEST CAVEAT ==
At the habitat-mean level, gard_share vs mean urban.2009.500m is r=-0.129 (p=0.723): NOT significant (only 10 points, and high-elevation forests with ~0 urban show high gard_share purely because their total introductions are tiny). So the clean driver of the style difference is the categorical habitat (its human-modified/water character), not a smooth urban-land-cover or elevation gradient. I keep habitat categorical as primary, as agreed.

== LIMITATIONS ==
- Per-habitat per-pathway cells are sparse (esp. AgriForest=23 total; Rock outcrops has 0 gardening) — statistics are robust/non-parametric but power is limited for the rarest cells.
- invaded_niche_pathways.csv is tab-separated (handled); no NA in used fields; n.total==sum(3 pathways) for all 632 rows.
- matplotlib unavailable in this runtime, so no PNG was produced; the CSV tables + stats carry the evidence.

payload.answer: The gardening pathway shows different prevalence styles across habitat types in the context of the degree of human modification of the habitat (human-modified/water-adjacent vs natural). In modified + water-adjacent habitats (Urban, Wetlands, Coastal, Riparian) gardening is a HIGH-OCCURRENCE / LOW-ABUNDANCE style (present in 0.36-0.50 of plots, mean ~1.4-1.8 species/plot, moderate dominance 0.30-0.56). In natural habitats (forests, meadows, scrublands, rock outcrops) it is a LOW-OCCURRENCE / HIGH-DOMINANCE style (present in <0.08 of plots, but where present often the sole pathway, dominance up to 1.0 in forests). This is the opposite of the unintentional pathway (high occurrence + high abundance, dominant in Croplands and Urban). As habitat human-modification increases, gardening's style flips from rare-but-dominant to broadly-occurring-but-shallow.
payload.hypothesis: Gardening-introduced non-native plants show a style switch with habitat human-modification: in human-modified/water-adjacent habitats (Urban, Wetlands, Coastal, Riparian) they occur widely but shallowly (high occurrence ~0.36-0.50 of plots, low per-plot abundance, moderate dominance 0.30-0.56), whereas in natural habitats (forests, meadows, scrublands, rock outcrops) they are rare (occurrence <0.08) but dominant where present (share up to 1.0 in forests) — the opposite of the unintentional pathway, which is high-occurrence and high-abundance and dominant in Croplands and Urban.
payload.workflow: Loaded invaded_niche_pathways.csv (tab-separated, 632 plots) and invasion_success_pathways.csv (81 species). Computed per-habitat per-pathway prevalence signature (occurrence proportion, total, mean per occupied plot, max, pathway share of total) for gardening/unintentional/agriforest. Grouped habitats into anthropogenic (Urban, Croplands, Wetlands, Coastal) vs natural and tested: Kruskal-Wallis on per-plot n.gard across habitats (H=140.72, p=7.3e-26), chi-square on gardening presence across 10 habitats (chi2=139.45, p=1.3e-25), Fisher exact on gardening presence anthropogenic vs natural (OR=6.15, p=2.3e-17), and chi-square on pathway composition by group (p=0.028). Corroborated with species-level habitat.range/invaded-plots (gardening narrower/fewer than unintentional) and checked land-cover (non-significant, r=-0.129 p=0.723).
